utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just very briefly apologise for my disappearance yesterday afternoon, but in the break, something came up in the Talic case, and that's why I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think how to proceed in the let's say next 90 minutes, and let's discuss whether or not we really can conclude today. We have to have a fair trial no doubt. And therefore, if necessary, we have to take the necessary time. May I ask, Document 25 -- Exhibit 259, is it prepared? Thank you. Do we have the best possible original available? As I can see no answer, I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, we're looking for it. You're asking for the evidence copy, the best original that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. So please let me know when it has arrived. May the usher, then, please escort witness Baltic into the courtroom. In the meantime, we can ask the registry to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, this is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Also, for the purpose of the transcript of this deposition, appearances of the OTP, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Baltic. May I ask the usher immediately to put Document 259 on the ELMO. Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start today, Mr. Baltic, I reviewed yesterday's transcript. And no doubt, you are a lawyer. You are effective in your rhetoric attempts, to put it very concrete, in order to avoid concrete answers. I think we shouldn't proceed this way. We don't have the time. Therefore, I would ask you to answer with a clear "yes" and"no" only if possible. And if not, concentrate, please, on the question. And if you didn't understand the question, please let me know. In addition, I have at this point in time only, once again, to recall that you are under a solemn declaration. And any kind of false testimony under solemn declaration would have severe consequences in this Tribunal as it is true in all jurisdictions in the world, as you know. You had some time to sleep over some of your answers. At the end of the day, I will come back to these issues where I have the impression that we might have got an incomplete or misleading answer from you. There are possibilities if you regard it as necessary to correct the one or other answer. We have Document 259 before us. And please, once again, the question: Did you sign this document on page 8? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the minutes that I looked at yesterday. And I told you that I couldn't see my signature on this document. It's not visible. Initially, I said that I was somewhat surprised to see that this was a copy because the number of the minutes should correspond to the number of the deputies. This was prepared for the session, and each deputy should have been given a copy of these minutes to see if there are any mistakes, any omissions, any objections, which are then corrected at the next session. So in addition to the minutes of the deputies, that the deputies have, the rest would go to the archives, to the files. That is why I'm not quite clear why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. The rules today are when I ask you a concrete question and ask you to answer with a clear yes or no, please do so. I asked: Did you sign this document on page 8? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we find that "I don't know" is also a legitimate answer. Maybe you should tell the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not for the Defence counsel to assist a witness. Please answer with a clear yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether I did or not, because I cannot see my real signature here. But it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we come back later on with other possible better readable copy or original of this document. The purpose of this exercise is, of course, not to trap you, only for your understanding. The original of this document is not available because it's in a laboratory and it will be here during the day. And therefore we will come back with this document. But as you mentioned, as you said, in principal, it's possible. Therefore, once again, could you now please explain why it was necessary that you under the words "Dr. Milomir Stakic, S. R," in addition you gave your maybe signature, and we can read in any event "sekretar, skupstine opstine, Dusan Baltic." Why this procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I found it a bit strange when I saw underneath that this was a copy. It would seem funny to have a copy of the minutes made. If this is a document, then it is officially signed and published by the relevant body. That is, the organ that is in charge of copying and signing the document. And then it can be considered as an official document. I don't know why it was necessary to make an additional copy because it must have been done in a large number of copies. It had been done already and distributed to the deputies, and not only the deputies, but everybody else who attended the session. This is just a piece of paper which is used by the deputies. It should enable the deputies to make sure that what they had discussed or proposed was indeed eventually adopted. If there were any omissions, then an objection to that effect would be made, and the appropriate correction done at the following session. So after each session, the minutes are distributed from the previous session for the following session. And it was in this manner that the accuracy of the copy was checked. And I failed to explain why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Let's proceed immediately. One document, whether this document or other documents, I understand from your answer in principle that it was a given possibility that you took -- by signing this document, or copies of this document, that to a certain degree, relying on assistants, other staff members, you mentioned legal officers, you took the responsibility for the correctness of this document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In general, not with special respect to the document before us, when you took this responsibility, did you take care that the document was indeed signed as it is written here "Dr. Milomir Stakic, S. R."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated that when publishing individual decisions in the Official Gazette, it was our practice that at the end of each decision, each individual decision, the name, that is, first of all, the title, the president of the Municipal Assembly, and the name of the president should be placed together with an abbreviation "S. R." which means "svojerucno," "in his own hand." However, this copy, this decision, was not signed. So a copy of the minutes of this kind would normally not be published in the Official Gazette. I think I addressed the issue yesterday. When you publish a decision of this kind in the Official Gazette, then you would have the same block as the one you can see here. And underneath, you also have the title of the secretary to the Municipal Assembly because he's a member of the technical services, technical personnel, who is acting as some sort of an editor. But when copying all of these decisions, and they constitute official documents, they have to be authentically reproduced in the Official Gazette, the way they are copied. And you are right; there is a responsibility for accuracy, but in order to fulfill this task completely, one would have to spend a huge amount of time and to check every -- everything, every single publication against the original and against the copy. And this was not the practice that we had. This is not what I did. Usually, whenever there was a mistake or an omission, there would be an immediate reaction by the deputies, and then in the next issue of the Official Gazette, a corrigendum would be published in a separate document. This is what I'm trying to emphasise. When I signed a document of this kind, I must say that I signed it with full confidence in the work of my associates because I never had any reason to think that they would put in something that was not actually said or should not have been there. In particular, when dealing with the minutes, the minutes constitute a separate -- a special kind of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. These kinds of documents, and I want -- don't want to refer only to Document 259, but in general, these kinds of documents, when it was under the rules or under the law necessary that a document be published, was this kind of document then sent to the Official Gazette, to Kozarski Vjesnik, to Glas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this was not the usual practice. I mean, it was not done on a regular basis. However, if sometimes we did proceed -- if sometimes this was indeed done, then -- I'm sorry, but I cannot remember any specific instance. Every session of the Municipal Assembly is a public event. Perhaps during the period of time when the Crisis Staff was operational, it was not public. I mean, the session was not broadcast over the radio. The citizens were not able to follow the work of the -- this body over the radio. But I really cannot remember any instance when we actually sent any decision to be published in the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this procedure of the publishing of decisions on the basis of other documents. Before we leave Document 259, no doubt the huge number doesn't allow -- or maybe didn't allow you to go into each and every detail of the document. But is it true that you participated in the meeting as such mentioned here? If you have, please, a look on page 1. If you please -- if I may draw your attention to the fifth paragraph, can you see your name there following the sentence "...took part in the decision preceding the adoption of the corrigendum..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, I can see my name in the penultimate sentence, penultimate line. Yes, as a participant in the discussion. This session took place in the month of August. We can see the date, the 27th of August. As I told you, the secretary normally attended the session of the assembly, together with the president and the vice-president. His presence was more formal in nature. If it was necessary, for instance, to provide an explanation on an issue or to point out if something was not in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Look, please, on page 2. There's I, the third paragraph, was there another person in among the assemblymen called Dusan Baltic, a person who is not identical with your person, or is it a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I or II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I, third paragraph, you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see, I. If I can have a moment, please, I cannot see very well. Yes, I've just read it. It says here: "The following took part in the debate, in the discussion." I don't know what it was that I discussed. I may have addressed the issue of the minutes. Actually, that was the only thing that I could have discussed because this is the portion where the minutes are discussed, that is, whether the minutes do entirely cover the work of the session. Maybe there was an objection to the effect that there had been an omission of some sort and attention was drawn to that fact. That could have been my intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it wasn't a mistake that it reads "Dusan Baltic"? There was not such a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not -- like I said, I indicated that it was my duty to attend the assembly sessions when it met in its regular, normal, composition. And whenever someone raised an issue regarding the minutes, then usually the debate -- a debate would follow as to whether there had been an omission or not. Those were the only contents that could have been discussed at this point at the meeting. But I can see that people here are deputies or persons in charge of individual municipal departments, in this paragraph, at least, I, paragraph 3. I already explained to you who these individuals are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally as regards this document from my side, may we turn to page 6, XIV, please. Can you please read it out that we can follow and we are on the safe side as regards the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Draft decision on the election of lay Judges in the municipal court in Prijedor, in the basic court in Prijedor. Introductory remarks were given by Dusan Baltic, secretary to the Municipal Assembly, and the following took part in the discussion: Milomir Stakic and Dragan Savanovic. The deputies reached the following conclusion unanimously: Area staffs should provide the list of person who could be elected as lay judges in the -- to the commission for election and appointments, if that has not been done so far, so that the commission could draft the proposal for the next session of the Municipal Assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's fair to conclude that also during the meeting as such, following these abridged minutes, you were present all the time and participated in your capacity as secretary in the meeting. Correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a debate concerning the appointments of lay judges to the lower court, which is within the competence of the Municipal Assembly. As far as I could tell from this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Once again, the question was: Did you participate all the time in this meeting in your capacity as secretary, in the meeting? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot remember that, but of course I was supposed to be present throughout the session. It is obvious that in this case, adequate preparations concerning these appointments had not been done. So probably it was necessary to explain why it was still not possible to go on with the appointments of lay judges. And that's why it was requested that the deputies, through the area staffs, which covered the areas of local communes, offered nominations of the people who could be appointed as lay judges. So a deadline was probably given for the written nominations to be submitted so that the issue can be decided upon on the following session. So that was the only explanation that I was able to provide at the time, that is, these steps had to be taken. There was a problem with the formal adoption of the decision, of the relevant decision, at this particular assembly because again, these are purely formal issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We may leave now Document S259. And may I ask the usher to present -- I'll give it to you -- Exhibit Number 180. And Official Gazette 2 of 1992, decision number 48. If both documents are please put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If Your Honour would prefer the evidence copy, the actual Gazette is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, yes. If the usher could take, once again, the best possible evidence. May we first, please, see the document, the other one. You can see this document, and you can see the header of this page. It reads there -- yes. Once again, Cyrillic, if you can help us out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see in the upper corner the words "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality, Crisis Staff. 17th of June, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And may we now turn to the signature we find on this document. Please, down at the end. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the right corner, we read: "President of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic." There is a signature as well, but I don't remember his signature, so I cannot identify it. It's probably his. I mean, it is my assumption that it is his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you see the words "S. R." or "Za" in front of the words Milomir Stakic? It maybe -- I have the impression covered by the stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is something here. It's either Za, Z-A, or "doctor" because as we could observe, his name is always preceded with the R, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only for the record, we had numerous stamps yesterday. What can we read in the stamp here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the stamp. The stamp reads as follows: "Socialist Republic" -- at least I think it reads "Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor Municipality, Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can now compare this document with the Official Gazette, is this document then published in the Official Gazette? Is it the same document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there is a difference because in this document, under the word "order," we can see four items, whereas on the screen, the document on the screen has five items. The original was published in the Official Gazette, and it bears the number and the date which cannot be seen -- which I cannot see, at least I cannot see the date on the document which is on the screen, nor can I see the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, show to the witness the number of both documents, and the witness may compare the numbers of both documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Here we can see better that the order which is on the screen contains four items. I don't want to read all of them. As is the case with this other document in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it the same number of decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I have -- in the document on the screen is the one that was published in the Official Gazette, and the number and the date correspond. As I indicated a moment ago, it was customary to place on the right side underneath "President of the Municipal Assembly" or "President of the Crisis Staff," in this case "Dr. Milomir Stakic," it is customary to put the abbreviation "SR" because normally, there was no signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. So could you now, on this basis, explain the way for a decision or order to be published in the Official Gazette from the building of the Municipal Assembly to, first of all, the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the usual procedure in all cases was at the end of the session to process the minutes of the session which meant that individual documents had to be prepared. These documents, as we have already mentioned, were delivered to the relevant organs. Following that, when there was a sufficient number of documents, that means the Official Gazette is not published after every single session; but rather, once there was a sufficient number of documents to be published. And then individual documents would be copied, typed, and were supposed to correspond with the original. Then all these documents were gathered, typed, and then from these typewritten versions would be used to produce a large number of Official Gazettes, a large number of copies of Official Gazettes. It was common practice to give this type of job to a company qualified to do this kind of job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who was in charge of -- yes, in modern words we would call this outsourcing, to ask another agency or company to prepare the Official Gazette or print the Official Gazette? Was it done in the building of the Municipal Assembly or in another building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier, at an earlier stage, as far as I can remember, this sort of job would be given to a company in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The name of this company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The company's Grad, Gradiska. They had a printing shop, and this was the sort of work they did, so they were quite capable of doing this kind of job, too. It was possible to do this also in -- with the administrative bodies in the building itself at the municipality. There were employees who performed the tasks of copying documents for the assembly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Also, it was possible to do this with one of the book binders or the printworks of the iron ore mining company, Ljubija, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have already heard there are several possibilities. But who ordered that? In a concrete case, it was done by this company or within the framework or in Ljubija? Who was responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Verifying the cheapest possibilities and the most convenient possibilities for doing this, whether it was cheaper and more convenient to have this done by the company in Gradiska or the mines, mainly we used the phone to obtain this sort of information. And that's when we decided to send this material - that was later the way they did it - to be copied, preprinted, and bound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Who is "we"? You said "we." Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to my collaborators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Baltic, is it true that you were head of the Municipal Assembly technical service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's proceed to another document. May I ask the usher to bring these documents back to those providing you with the documents. And turn to Exhibit S76 and Official Gazette 299, Number 44. Can you please have a special look on the number of the decision and the first two lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean decision number in the upper left corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number is 02-111-180/92. The 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then in the first line, it reads, and it appears to be that there is a handwritten addendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see any handwritten addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the third word, something is added.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that. That's in the line above the word "decision pursuant to Article 7" and then something was added, a mark was added in handwriting. I think it reads "3," decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may we now immediately turn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe something was added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to the Official Gazette, and if you could compare the number and the first line. Is it the same number of the decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the upper corner, following the word "decision," it says: "Pursuant to Article" -- I can't see clearly. I think it's 3 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does it correspond with what we just saw before, that before the number 7, it was added in handwriting as 3.I. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you compare these two, what I'm looking at now, that's an individual decision. This was not extracted from the Official Gazette. If I compare, I see that this text here contains no corrections, the one on the screen. And the one I'm looking at, the one I'm holding in my hand, I can see that there's a handwritten addition, item 3. Maybe it was omitted at first, and then someone reinserted Article 3 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Baltic, is it correct that what we can see in the Official Gazette reflects the start of the sentence as we can read it from the other document including the inserted 3.I. Is it correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are differences here. I see that here, there are three lines in this decision on the screen, if that's what was published in the Official Gazette. While in the other decision, you only have two lines. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Sorry to interrupt. We are not interested whether it's here three and there are two lines. We are interested in the content and nothing else. If you could read it word by word, is it the same wording including this added 3.I or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that the text itself is the same. Aside from the omitted number 3, which was then added in handwriting. The other words correspond with -- are the same in both copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then turn to other documents, please, which is Exhibit 70, 7-0, and Official Gazette 2 of 1992. And, yes, leave it with this first. If you can only compare this document, please show us the signature on this document. Once again, for the purpose, we have several stamps. Which stamp is it? What can we read in the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that this stamp is identical to the one before, the one I have also read out. It reads: "Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Prijedor Municipal Assembly, Prijedor." So this I think would be the stamp that had been used up to, and then later there appeared the stamp saying "Crisis Staff." So this was the previous stamp. I don't know how, if in the same period of time, two different stamps appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then, please compare just the document you have before you in the Official Gazette and the other document. Does the Official Gazette reflect this document, the 6th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the one displayed on the screen or the one I'm looking at? I didn't quite understand you. This is a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the ELMO, or the apparatus is not big enough to have both on them. If you would be so kind and compare both documents, the Official Gazette, and the one which is now on the apparatus. May the usher please give the document from the ELMO to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the two texts are identical, as well as the number and date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So just for the record, could you please repeat the number and date you read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number and date of the decision published in the Official Gazette is the 6th of June, 1992, and the number is 02-111-146/92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present the colour copy of this document, S70, to the witness. Mr. Baltic, have you seen these kinds of decisions or order beforehand in the way you can see it now in the colour version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have never seen a decision with a stamp and a signature of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood you well. I thought you'd asked whether I've seen a decision in colour, in colour print. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Whether you have seen this document reflected in this and copied here in colour in original version. These documents of this kind in your capacity as secretary and head of technical service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have stated earlier that minutes of meetings of the Crisis Staff were kept in handwriting by a recording clerk who wrote the minutes down in the book of minutes. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to override once again. The question was: Have you seen original documents with original stamp, original signature, of that kind of document you have before you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have never seen a document with a stamp and signature of Dr. Stakic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps earlier, but during the work of the Crisis Staff, the decisions that were typewritten, the same recording clerk's typist who compiled the minutes and the assistants as before, drafting of individual -- the preparing of individual decisions. When they were prepared, they were handed in for signature by the same people, and they were forwarded by the people I worked with. There were no questions for me -- no one raised issues of anyone failing in their duties in my service so that I would have been in a position to take measures against these people. So this was -- the same thing was done always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So one can conclude from your testimony that there's no reasonable doubt that these documents were authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I say that was the procedure. And these should be -- because the procedure earlier and during the operation of the Crisis Staff was the same, so these documents should be original documents. And they were supposed to be published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to a more general question: By the example, two examples, three examples, we came to the conclusion these decisions, orders, were printed in the Official Gazette. We have in our documents Official Gazettes starting with number 1, 2, 3 of 1992. Were there any kind of change in the Official Gazette after the 30th of April in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for a while. That is, as I've said before, decisions were published in the Official Gazette also in the preceding period. But also during the period of the operation of the Crisis Staff. And whenever there was a sufficient number of decisions to warrant publication of the Official Gazette, it would not be logical for the Official Gazette to be prepared and published after every single session because that would not have been economical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is there any special reason that the -- that number 1 of the Official Gazette - this is Exhibit 276 - dates the 20th of May, 1992? Were there no publications between 1st of January and the 20th of May, 1992? Maybe it helps if I can show you the cover page of the Official Gazette of 20 May, Number 1, 1992. As said before, Exhibit 276. Would you please be so kind and have a look on this document. Was this the beginning of a new era because it reads in the beginning: "Pursuant to Article 12 of the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Prijedor Municipal Assembly at its session held on 20th May, 1992, adopted the following decision on implementation of decisions and other regulations of Prijedor Municipality."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you brighten it up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may have a look on the apparatus beside you. It's better for you. You can read it better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read the decision, and I can see that the introductory part before the actual decision, reference is made to Article 12 of the constitutional law for the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was pursuant to that particular article that the Prijedor Municipal Assembly adopted the decision on the implementation of decisions and other regulations of the Prijedor Municipality. This is some sort of instruction destined to the administrative organs so that they would know what regulations they are supposed to apply. The decision concerned all employees of the municipal administrative bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry once again to override. The question was and still is: Does the fact that we have a new Number 1 of the Official Gazette as of May and starting with these remarkable words reflect a new start, a new era, in Prijedor or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this decision, we can see that the Prijedor Municipal Assembly was still working, and not the Crisis Staff. But if you have a look at the upper portion of the document, you will see that the legal basis for the adoption of this decision was the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic. This had all -- this was already mentioned, I think, when you made reference to the region, the region of Krajina. This was in May. I cannot remember at this point the specific decisions where reference was made to AR Krajina, to their regulations. Here, reference is made to the constitution of the Serbian Republic and not to the Krajina. This is the period of time preceding the disagreement, that is, the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You recall a document you saw yesterday as of August 1992 stating that you and others were employed as from 7 January, 1992. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should like to have a look at it again in order to be able to provide a precise explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit Number 262. And to have it in the context, because there is reflected what the attachments are, the cover page in Cyrillic and - please wait - one list mentioned there. To be very concrete, does this mean that as of 7 January, 1992, you worked for a period up to four years, as we can read it there, as the secretary, Municipal Assembly of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Serbia Assembly of Prijedor Municipality? Correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have stated on previous occasions, that I, as the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, as a member of the technical services, worked from the January 1991 -- the 1st of January, 1991, until early March 1993, which means that I was the head of this particular technical service throughout that period of time. Here, in this list of officials, the one that I have in front of me, the list of the officials of the assembly contains the names of these officials, and we can see who the secretaries were. The directors are also mentioned here. For example, the director of the tax administration, the municipal tax administration. All these people are people who were in charge of specific municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was only related to your person. You are the witness here. And the cover sheet of this document, in its heading reads: "Serbian Republic Krajina, Autonomous Region, Prijedor Municipal Assembly, Election and Appointments Commission, date, 8 September 1999." And then, in the final paragraph: "We have enclosed a list of officials appointed by the assembly." And this list, you have in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. The date is the 8th of September, 1992. But as far as I can recall, the Crisis Staff did not exist at the time, that is, on the 8th of September, 1992. We have seen the minutes on the confirmation of the decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff. This happened in July, and here, we see that this was in September, that is, at the time when the regular assembly was able to convene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Sorry to override once again. The question is not Crisis Staff or not Crisis Staff. We are discussing now the issue of Serbian Republic, Krajina Autonomous Region, Prijedor Municipal Assembly. Enclosed are a list of officials appointed by the assembly in January 1992. Is it true that you were appointed in this capacity specially for these purposes in January 1992? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January 1992, I was still the secretary of the assembly, that is, the multiethnic assembly if I might call it that way. The president of the assembly was Cehajic, and the vice-president was Savanovic -- sorry, Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this document is a list of officers in charge, that is, the officials, who had been appointed by the Municipal Assembly. I don't see the date when this review, this list, was made. If it was the -- part of this document dated on the 8th of September, I don't know. Then only the information as to who these officials are is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think all participants can draw their own conclusions from your line of answers. Let me turn to another issue, and may I once again ask the usher, please, to be so kind and remove this document and to put this document on the ELMO, please, which is S208, Kozarski Vjesnik. You see the Kozarski Vjesnik. I think it's better to have it -- to read it on the apparatus beside you. It's easier to read. Can you please read out the entire title of this newspaper, including the stamp printed on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see here that this is an issue of Kozarski Vjesnik, and the title is "A Lesson For Future." And then an information to the readers, "A Ban on Entry and Leaving the Town, and an Appointment for the Commission for Assessment of Damage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the word Kozarski Vjesnik, above the word --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What can you read there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see highlighted in green, we read the words "war edition." Are you asking me whether I know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Now you may turn a little bit lower to the right-hand side, there you can see a marked announcement on the time schedule of buses leaving Prijedor. Apparently a decision by, yes, in the framework of your work, taken by the Municipal Assembly or Crisis Staff, whatever. But the way -- I'm only interested in the way how was -- were decisions transferred or proceeded to Kozarski Vjesnik? Was it also in your office, in your capacity of secretary or head of technical services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had -- I haven't had an opportunity of seeing an edition of this kind of Kozarski Vjesnik so far. But it is possible that pursuant to a request issued by the president of the assembly, the decisions adopted by the assembly were published by the papers. It was up to him and up to his assessment of the situation. As to which particular decisions should be sent out, this was done through the employees of technical services, that is, my coworkers. These decisions usually went out without prior consultations with me because that was the prerogative of the president. He was able to ask Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any of the employees of the technical services to provide him with a document or to have a document sent out. The vice-president, the deputy president, had the same right as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I see it correctly that 259 is available now in the best possible original? Could the last page please be put on the ELMO. Once again, only one final question once more: On the basis of this document, your signature? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The signature is not clearly visible. I'm not saying that the document was not signed, but I cannot see my signature on this document. I would also like to see the preceding portion of the text because I said that I did attend some of the sessions. Whether I attended this particular one, I don't know. I don't know which session here we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Discussed already earlier, we went through portions, so we shouldn't come back to this. Now how to proceed. Mr. Baltic, you saw that unfortunately I took longer than expected, and unfortunately even after the break -- maybe it also serves your interest -- I have to have -- to put eight or nine questions to you. But no doubt, the parties have the right to put -- also to put questions to you. And I'm afraid it will not be possible to do this by the end of the day. Tomorrow, there's no courtroom available. So this would mean that we would kindly ask you to stay here until Monday. Would you be prepared to do so? Of course, all the expenses as regards accommodation and so on are covered by the Victim and Witness Section of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that I would be able to travel back today. I accepted your invitation. But it would be more suitable for me if it could be arranged so that we work longer today so that my testimony could be completed by the close of the day so I could travel back tomorrow because I have a number of commitments and a lot of work to do, the kind of work that cannot be postponed, that also entails certain expenses. So once again, it would be preferable if we could work longer today so that the testimony could be completed because staying until Monday would be too long for me. So if there is a possibility of preceding in that manner, I would kindly ask the Court to...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because as you also indicated, you are not sitting -- I myself don't need any breaks to carry on. Maybe we can work longer, the way we did yesterday, so that we can try and complete the testimony today. Once again, I kindly ask the Court to understand me, to understand my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand quite well that it would be preferable, and we will try to do our best. But please understand that not only for the Prosecutor, but first of all, I think in this case, for the Defence, it's absolutely mandatory to have a fair procedure and have a fair trial, that the time is not too limited. And therefore, take it we try our very best, but in case, be prepared that it may be necessary that we continue on Monday. Let's have a break now until 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, before the witness is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please take care the witness is not brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can come in. That's okay. There's nothing to be hidden. You should meet three people, potential witnesses, coming from Canada for Monday and Tuesday, and it has been prearranged because we don't have time to go to Canada in between our cases, and my co-counsel is preparing military experts, so he does not have time to prepare this witness. So we would like to have this witness finished today as well if possible. We are ready to stay longer, and we think that our 90 minutes is enough for us to finish. So we would like and ask you kindly to consider if possible to finish with this witness today, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the Prosecution? What is the estimated time you think is necessary for your questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian is going to cross-examine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's not -- I had a discussion with our president on this issue. I don't -- let's call it not examination-in-chief or cross-examination, to put questions to the witness in addition. So what will be the necessary time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We estimate two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So indeed, it could be possible that we all take care, on the basis of what we did yesterday, one additional hour we could proceed. If all the participants, yes, in the light of enabling us to have no court tomorrow and let the witness go back to his home country, that we try to have one additional hour today. I can see already that Ms. Dahuron preparing the necessary. Thank you, may the witness be brought in now. In the meantime, Mr. Baltic, we have discussed the possibilities how to enable that we can conclude today. And the best contribution by your side can be to answer as short and as precise as possible. Before starting with my final line of questions, once again to draw your attention to the indication that as it is usual under international law, we have granted safe conduct to you. This means that you do not have to be afraid that anything, any initiative, would be taken against you on the basis whatever may have happened prior to your arrival to The Hague. This is covered by the letter of safe conduct, and it's granted also by the Netherlands. So there, you shouldn't be afraid. But on the other hand, you have to be aware that this safe conduct doesn't cover a possible procedure if one party or the Bench or one of the Judges could come to the conclusion that there might be in part false testimony. Therefore, please be aware of this and try to give detailed, short but truthful answers. When looking back to this period of time, who, in your assessment, was at that time your boss, to put it this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The secretary of the assembly is elected by the assembly. And the assembly can dismiss me or relieve me of my duty. It is from the assembly that I receive the decision on my appointment. If I fail in my duties, if I fail to perform my duties, in the opinion of the deputies, there would be an initiative to relieve me of my duties. In that sense, my superior is the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the assembly represented by whom? I think it's, as it is always, there were day-to-day questions arising, and no doubt you can't ask the entire assembly. In this sense, who was your boss?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I understood your question, the president of the assembly is a deputy, just like the vice-president. If I failed in organising in a proper way the work of the technical services, it would be the president, as the deputy, or the vice-president -- the vice-president or any other deputy, not necessarily in a decision-making position, could start the initiative to relieve me of my duty and to dismiss me from my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So whenever you had a day-to-day question, you approached whom and asked, "How shall I proceed?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, concerning certain issues, legal issues, concerning with the procedure of the assembly's operation were reviewed and discussed with my colleagues. Those were procedural matters. If someone resigns, for example, and it needs to be discussed at the assembly, I usually consulted my colleagues how this can be dealt with. I hope you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to override once again. You mentioned your colleagues. Can you please attach names to your colleagues, what you regard as your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My colleagues were Zdravka Vranic, and Radmila Majkic, both lawyers, and a political scientist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Baltic, we shouldn't play around. To be concrete, was Dr. Stakic your boss? Whenever you had some questions you couldn't resolve amongst your colleagues, did you ask for the advice or directions of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Advice and instructions, he couldn't give me advice or instructions because he is a doctor by profession. There were no such matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Isn't it true that Dr. Stakic was president of the Municipal Assembly and not acting there as a physician? Please don't try to escape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is nothing I'm trying to escape from. He is the president of the municipality, and he has the right to summon me if he feels that there is a need to talk to me about something concerning the operation of the assembly. What was at stake was the schedule of the sessions and the possibility to use certain rooms, certain halls, to hold the sessions. And whatever else was connected with the assembly would previously have been discussed at a meeting of the executive committee. Whenever there was an issue - I can't think of any specific issues now - I would be obliged to respond to the call and to see what the issue was. And if I was not myself qualified to deal with the issue, I was supposed to bring it up with my colleagues and analyse the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Baltic, what would be your assessment? Was there, following the 7th or maybe the 9th of January, 1992, only one Municipal Assembly, or something one could call a shadow Municipal Assembly, the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Municipality of Bosnia-Herzegovina [sic]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a question that I have never been asked, but you can tell from the documents that the assembly was regulated but did not function. Up until -- I can't say precisely when, whether it was late May or if it was envisaged, regulated somewhere, at some point in the period you referred to, in January, it did not operate. It began to operate in late May and early June. If you look at the decision on the establishment of the Crisis Staff, you can see that it was established on the 20-something of May, in the second half of May. At any rate, around the 25th, I think, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, we shouldn't confuse two notions, Crisis Staff and Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Was a Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor created in January 1992, to the best of your recollection and as indicated in this document that you, acting as from this point in time as secretary to this Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify this point. This assembly presided over by the president of the assembly, such as Stakic, it dated back to the period around late April or May, roughly speaking. And up to that point, there had been a multiethnic assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was such a Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, having held a session in the public utilities company hall at 17 hours, the 16th of April, 1992, ERN Number 03024253, included in Exhibit S262? Are you aware of this meeting of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I recall that particular meeting precisely. But as I've said, if you look at that document, you can see who the new president of the assembly was and who the vice-president was. If we talk about the Serbian Municipal Assembly, when the assembly members were being elected and I was referred to as the secretary, I was not invited to that particular meeting. But I remained to perform my duties as the head of the technical services, merely the administrative part connected with the work of the assembly. This may have been about, well, January, if that date, the dates don't quite seem to make sense to me. I see that some things were published later on, but that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's leave it with this. You worked for about two years and three months in the Municipal Assembly. Who played de facto the leading role in the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word itself, the president of the Municipal Assembly, speaks for itself because he was the one who presided over the assembly and made decisions to the effect whether the assembly would be convened and also decisions concerning the agenda. From -- what was required from that position, the technical services completed their technical part of the work. There was also a possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. To be once again quite concrete, we know very well that in some countries, municipalities, towns, you have a president but de facto the deputy, or in, yes, some former Soviet Union countries, even the secretary played a major role than the president itself. How was it in Prijedor? Was it as it was laid down in the rules and in the law that, indeed, the president of the Municipal Assembly was the one who had the say, or was there any other person who directed within Prijedor this president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the assembly, the chairman of the assembly, worked together with the chairman of the executive board. And the executive board would previously have discussed all the issues and sent their proposals to the president with the recommendation to have these issues discussed at the assembly. The statute of the assembly envisages of the respective fields' areas of competence of the president, the secretary, the vice-president, the chairman of the executive board, and the members of the executive board. You can see in the statute that in Prijedor, and the situation was much the same in all the other municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... We want to conclude today. Was there any stronger person in the Municipal Assembly than Dr. Stakic, de facto? One thing is what we call de jure, and the other is de facto. Was there such any stronger person who had maybe the say in the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this is not the best way to put it, but as the deputies and the president of the assembly was also a deputy, after all, they were proposed, nominated, by their respective parties in case they were politicians to begin with. And then at the party level, there must have been debates as to who would be nominated for a specific range of positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, once again to override, I don't want to discuss party issues. I want to discuss that what you experienced in the Municipal Assembly being seated beside the president when there was an ordinary Municipal Assembly meeting. Who was the leading person? Was it the president, as seen in the rules, or was it everybody else? Was it the president? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The following three questions are -- have the purpose to give the possibility to correct maybe misleading answers or answers that were not understood correctly. Yesterday, on transcript page 76, line 10 to 16, it reads: "I'm not a member of the SDS." Mr. Baltic, have you been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Nor did I attend the sessions. As I have already indicated, when my name was proposed for the position of the secretary, an acquaintance of mine called me on the telephone asked me whether I was willing to take the job. And I told you the reasons why I accepted the job; I was unemployed at the time. No one had the grace to ask me whether I was willing to do it or not. I mean, I am referring to the people who were proposing the candidates. And as you know, the SDS and SDA participated with their delegates in the assembly. Had I been a member of the SDS, the issue would have been discussed beforehand, and I would have been in a position to be informed of that possibility by the members of the party. Somebody would have asked me if I was willing to do it or not, but in this way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... You maybe go one step too far. Would documents lie? If, for example, the document I have before me on 7 May, 1991, Minutes of the Meeting of the Committee for Adopting the Annual Budget of the SDS Municipal Board, it reads, "Committee Members: One, Milan Dragojevic; two, Ranko Radanovic; three, Dusan Kurnoga; four, Dusko Baltic." Would the book of minutes lie when in the meeting of the Prijedor SDS municipal board as of 20 March, 1991, page 3 of the minutes, page 5 of the minutes one can read, Contributions Assigned -- evidently to your person. Are all these documents untrue? There's nothing wrong to be a member of the SDS and it's not punishable. It's only to give you the possibility to correct that what you stated yesterday in order to avoid any consequences for you. And it's mandatory for a presiding officer, judge in this case, to alert you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand you. But so that you can understand me, I have to add that the parties who participated in the government had distributed the functions, not only of the Municipal Assembly but other functions as well. There were talks between the parties as to these positions and offices where political parties did not have their people, these positions would be offered to nonmembers. And it was the municipality that financed the political parties who participated in the government. But they also -- the municipality also financed the parties in general. And it was possible for them to call me up and to discuss the issue. I was, after Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. all, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, and it was my duty to work equally with everybody. So I would from time to time be invited for that purpose. As for the appointments to certain positions, then I as a technical person, a technical member of the assembly was often called to attend and to provide opinion as to the procedural aspect of the appointment, to see, for example, whether the adequate requirements are fulfilled by the candidate and so on and so forth. And I was the one who gave the opinion as to the statutory regulations regarding these appointments. So I would attend such meetings of all the three parties if invited. That was one of my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your testimony you participated -- I don't know whether also in meetings of other parties, but you participated in SDS meetings but you never were a member of the SDS. The final question, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I've just confirmed it, but only in respect of these issues, the one that I described concerning the appointments and the financing of the parties and appointments to a number of positions including the position of school directors and company directors because there was an interparty agreement which provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... With a view to the watch. Once again, the question to be answered with a clear yes or no, have you been a member of the SDS? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of any party. I was not involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said yesterday that you never saw Dr. Stakic in uniform in the municipal building. We have before us the testimony of at least one witness telling us that this person saw Dr. Stakic in camouflage uniform in his office. We have seen yesterday, the day before, and the day before on video Dr. Stakic wearing uniform. Is it possible that during the night you recall, in looking back, that indeed you saw Dr. Stakic wearing a uniform, or is it still your testimony that opposed to this witness and video we saw, you never saw Dr. Stakic in uniform? Did you see him in uniform ever? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that last time, the way I understood you was whether Dr. Stakic came to work in uniform. However, now I must say that the Crisis Staff which functioned at that time, which used to be called the war presidency, they did have uniforms that they wore when they visited the soldiers because from time to time, such visits were organised for the purpose of taking food or parcels to the soldiers. So if such a visit was organised on that particular day, it is possible that he showed up to the municipal building in uniform. But that I saw him coming to work dressed that way, that it was his working uniform, no. I mean, it was not an obligation for them to wear the uniform that they possessed at the time. They did not have to wear it to work; but if they went to visit the troops, then they would go dressed in uniforms. But that was not only the case with Dr. Stakic but with other members of the Crisis Staff as well. As I've already explained, the body was initially called the war presidency, and then it was renamed Crisis Staff. But it's one and the same thing. So I'm not excluding the possibility that the witness in question could have seen him dressed that way. It is possible that it happened on the day when such a visit was organised. I went to the office of the president only when and if necessary. He had a different set of coworkers and colleagues, people he worked with. He contacted me only when an issue concerning the work of the assembly was discussed. As I told you, it was not a uniform that was typically worn every day, and the same applied to everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you stated that by chance, at the same time, you left the office in maybe February or March - you left it open - 1993, and at the same time Dr. Stakic was substituted by another person. We have witness statement on transcript page 4169, starting but then concrete question on the following page, which is 4170. The question was: "Do you know that Dr. Stakic was fired from the position of the president of the municipality in October 1992?" Answer: "I know that he was fired, but I don't know the reason. I know that he was replaced by a man called Kurnoga." Could you please concentrate on this question once again. Are you sure that it was indeed in February, March, or may it even have happened that he was "fired" already in autumn 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was present at this session when Mr. Stakic resigned. Whether he resigned under pressure -- but you can perhaps draw your conclusions from the following. It was very difficult to convene the session for several months as a result of interpersonal problems, and I am referring to the new set of people who had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. The question is: Was it in February or March 1993, or in autumn 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1992. I began working for my old company on the 1st of March, thereabouts. So it must have been a matter of several days. I remember that it was not possible to continue with the work of the session. There was a break at one point in time. We waited to see what would happen, and then he showed up and it was a surprise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... At this moment but not in order to stop you, but it reads on the transcript: "It was in 1992." Did you want to say "it was in 1992" or did you want to say "in 1993"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. It was in 1993. My apologies, Your Honour. It was in 1993, in late February or early March. That is what I had in mind. If I said in 1992, I misspoke. That could not have been the case. I indicated earlier that the issue was the use of resources and the humanitarian aid, and Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Miskovic, Mr. Kurnoga, Dusan, who would later become the president of the assembly, insisted that he be replaced. However, the deputies did not vote his relief of duty. It was his written request, his written resignation which the deputies then used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. But I take it your testimony is what we have heard yesterday, and you make reference to your testimony of yesterday. And there, you went already into details. I think this has been clarified. And just to round up, the final question: In the beginning of your testimony, you stated: "I received an offer from an acquaintance to be assigned as secretary." Could you please name this acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the party, Topic, Gojko Topic was his name, SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes my line of questions. And the floor is now for the Prosecution, please. Questioned by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, you told us that you were appointed as the secretary to the multiethnic Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and began in January 1991 and continued until the 1st of March, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that I was elected to the position of the secretary of the multiethnic assembly and that I worked for that multiethnic assembly. Once it ceased working, I remained as a member of technical services, to continue with my work. I couldn't abandon my position. All of the clerks who were employed there, 200 or 300 of them, also stayed. And I worked until March 1993 as such whereupon I started working for my original company, the flat council -- construction council. As to this particular session, the one that happened in late February or early March, that was the session when Stakic resigned, although it was requested that the deputies relieve him of duty because of the distribution of resources and the humanitarian aid which was abundant at the time. Because according to some rumours, every citizen of Prijedor should have received five tonnes of humanitarian aid. And then of course the question was asked who took those funds? Who took that aid? And then Garaca, Srdo [sic], the representative of the Red Cross, the local Red Cross who I believe distributed this aid on his own was in conflict with these other people who were dissatisfied with the situation. So a disagreement occurred, a rift occurred, and they wanted a new set of individuals to come to the assembly. And this is what happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe earlier this morning, you indicated you wanted to go home this week. If you want to do that, please try to confine your answer to the question that I ask. I appreciate the information you've volunteered, but you won't go home if you continue to volunteer information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your position, did anyone ever complain about the work that you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were complaints. It was Srdo Garaca who complained. But the reasons were of personal nature. He wanted to secure a lot for the construction of a building. And I said: "Why didn't you do it before when the lots were distributed?" And he said: "You can no longer stay at this position." And I said: "Well, I don't have to remain at this position." He probably didn't like me. There were two other occasions when more or less the same thing happened. He threatened me. He said that I will ask for your removal. Everything was, as I said, very personal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, the person that you're calling Srdo -- I believe you used a name like Garaca, is that Srdo Srdic, a deputy to the parliament in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Srdo Srdic, yes. Yes, that's correct. He was a deputy. I apologise. I confused the family name. Srdo Srdic, whom we all called "dentist" though he was just a dental assistant. There should not be any mistake about his identity, that was Srdo Srdic who was a deputy in the assembly. Whether he was the president of the SDS at the time, I don't know. But he was for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you resigned following a conflict with Mr. Srdic, the same as Dr. Stakic resigned following a conflict with Mr. Srdic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason why I left was not of the same kind. People were dissatisfied with my work. And then, things being as they were, it all culminated, and I realised that I couldn't work with any of these people, nor with the deputies who were actually the ones who made decisions as to who would work. But let me explain: The new people even apologized to me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If -- again, if you want to finish today, please confine your answer to the question. Did the presidents of the municipality whom you worked with, that is, Muhamed Cehajic, Milomir Stakic, did they ever complain about the quality or quantity of your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cehajic didn't complain about my work while he was the president, nor did Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe you indicated a moment ago to His Honour, Mr. President, that the technical services sector had about 200 or 300 employees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the technical services. I was referring to the entire municipal administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many employees worked for the technical service under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact number, but it was around seven, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had an office, you indicated, approximately 10 metres from that of the president of the municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The offices were located at the same location where they used to be. Before I came after Radmila Vrankic, who was the former secretary, she handed over the keys to the office and the desk, and I also took over everything that was -- all the material that was in this office. I trusted Mrs. Vrankic because she remained to work for the services as a legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question again is: Your office was approximately 10 metres from that of the president of the municipality? In other words, you -- your door, was as close to that of the president of the municipality as perhaps you are now from where I am. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a corridor between us. I entered my office from the right, and the entrance to his office was from the lobby. The distance between our two doors was 10 to 15 metres approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in January of 1992, approximately one year after you began to work for the assembly, a new assembly was formed of solely SDS deputies. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. I believe I've already said that. I personally did not attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't attend the session when this was decided. As I told you, I was not a member of any party. I was just filling in the position of the secretary which office belonged to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were appointed by the SDS to a position that was one of the more important positions in the municipality of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said. That is, that the political parties had distributed the offices of the assembly. So the office of the secretary of the assembly went to the SDS. The HDZ had a number of positions as well, but they were fewer in numbers. This policy also applied to the directors of local companies. Offices of company directors were also distributed amongst the parties. So the SDS was in a position to propose me or someone else for this position if they wanted to have the job done properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we won't finish with you until Monday if you give long answers to questions that you can give short answers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had no experience prior to being appointed working with an assembly. You told us you were not a politician. And yet, you were appointed to this position which was allotted solely to the SDS party. And you don't know why. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was appointed because I'm a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you did attend some of the meetings of the Serbian assembly in Prijedor -- or excuse me. I take that -- let me begin again. You told us that you did attend -- you told Your Honour that you did attend meetings of the SDS party, but you did that because it was your job to help all parties and all factions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I attended the sessions of the commission, not the meetings of the party. I'm referring to the commission for personnel matters. Whenever they had a problem, a legal problem, which they couldn't resolve, if they needed a legal explanation, then they would call me and I would attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the SDA, the HDZ, or any of the left parties in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not invited. But I did attend the meetings of deputies' clubs. There were a number of issues to be resolved. So in order to deal with it quickly, it was said that all deputies' clubs should assemble and reach an agreement, and that in this they should be assisted by the secretary of the assembly. There was an issue concerning urban planning, and I was in the club of the SDA deputies because they had the greatest number of deputies. And I provided an explanation to their questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after the formation of the Serbian assembly of Prijedor in January of 1991 [sic] or before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I've just told you about, the urban planning regulation and plan, that was in the period before, earlier. I think it was in 1991, whether in late 1991 I think so, but I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the SDS party began to boycott the assembly, did you also stop going to meetings of the assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the Serb deputies walked out, you remained and worked with President Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You had to see to it that the assembly formally -- well, an assembly is an assembly. If there is a quorum, it must continue to operate no matter if one of the parties walk out. But if there is no quorum, I would be there to warn them that there was not a sufficient number of members present and that the session could not be held. So then they would stop, too, if there was no quorum. So I stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea or any discussions with Mr. Topic about the position that you were offered or getting a job from the SDS prior to the phone call when he told you you were already appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He phoned me after a session of the main board of the SDS where the issue of nominations for the position of the secretary was debated. In their party, they did not have any lawyers, so they came up with people who were not members of the party --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My question related only to whether you spoke to Mr. Topic or anyone else from the SDS about getting a job from them prior to receiving the phone call from Mr. Topic. Did you or did you not speak to anyone from the SDS before they told you you were selected as the secretary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I was told over the phone that I would be nominated, and that's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
