utterances.text: Your job as the secretary of the assembly and in charge of the technical service was -- the most important part was helping to prepare Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the agenda for the deputies of the assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't actually decide on the agenda; that was under the law, the municipal statute, and that was the function of the president of the municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would have to coordinate with him and follow his instructions as to the agenda that he wanted for the upcoming meetings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received a proposal for the agenda because it had been agreed in cooperation with the executive committee who worked on the proposal. And he, too, attended the sessions whenever he could. They told him about it, they informed him. And I already had the agenda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when the assembly reached decisions or conclusions or orders, it was part of your duties to see that they were distributed and published. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once the work of the assembly was finished, then typists would use the tape recordings to typewrite minutes. And then decisions would be prepared individually, and the staff of the technical services enjoyed our full trust. And then afterwards, they would be stamped and signed by the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, in addition to your job as the secretary of the assembly, you also held the position of the editor of the Official Gazette of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the statute, the secretary is also the editor. Formally, what that meant is that underneath the decisions published in the Official Gazette, it reads who the president was and you also had the name of the editor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout 1992, did you continue to work? Did you go to your office Monday through Friday and keep regular hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The year 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said before, up until March 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work with the Crisis Staff? Was it part of your duties to assist the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was not a member of the Crisis Staff, although earlier in the statute, where it says "war presidency," the secretary was a member of the war presidency. But when the Crisis Staff was established, I asked not to be included as a member of that sort of staff. I didn't think there was a need to be included. You can look at the decision and clearly see for yourself the secretary is simply not one of the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it that you did not want to be a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believed that as the head of the technical services of the assembly, I should see to my own tasks. And in the statute, it said before that the secretary was not to be a member of the Crisis Staff because the secretary was not a political appointment itself but merely technical assistance. Prior to the assembly meetings and following the assembly meetings, the secretary was not a decision-maker. He was technical support. So that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever do any military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do military service?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Bosnia, from 1992 through 1995, did you perform any military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No military service. I did not even have a uniform or a weapon, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you told us you were born in 1941. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us why when almost all Serbs who were able to work were mobilised you were not mobilised in 1992? Was it because of the position that you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All higher officials and directors of companies were supposed to be in their -- to remain in their positions in order to preserve the organisation and the work of companies. So they could not go anywhere unless they wanted to themselves of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this, sir: You told us that you weren't a member of the Crisis Staff, that they didn't include you in their meetings normally, that you didn't publish their decisions until the Municipal Assembly reconvened. But you told us that you went to work every day and conducted normal hours. What were you doing from the takeover, on the 30th of April, 1992, until the Municipal Assembly began to reconvene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not understand me clearly. I said I was not a member of the Crisis Staff but whenever I was called upon to attend as someone providing technical support, yes, I may have been present. But only when invited. Decisions that were made were very brief. At the early stage, they were not delivered in writing to members of the Crisis Staff. They were just put forward orally, proposals, and they would be recorded into a minute book, handwritten by a recording clerk. And then this recording clerk later on would help the people -- the typists who compiled the minutes. Individual decisions were then prepared the way that they were recorded in the minutes. Or if that wasn't possible, so if that was from an organ of administration, if an expert opinion was needed for that particular area of competence, for that field, to correct perhaps the wording of the decision, then that decision would be stamped and delivered to wherever it was necessary. And later on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're saying is interesting, but we'll come back to that. So if I understand your answer, you're telling us that your assistance and invitation to the Crisis Staff to attend their meetings kept you busy, that it was the equivalent of a full-time job. Is that correct? What did you do when you attended the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply sat there. And if there were any legal matters to be clarified when drafting decisions, my duty was to assist and explain whether it was possible pursuant to the existing laws to pass a certain decision. And I did everything else, too, except I didn't pick up the agenda myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as a lawyer attending and giving legal advice to the Crisis Staff, did you discuss the detention of citizens of Prijedor such as the former mayor, Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please just repeat the question for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. You've told us that the Crisis Staff asked you for legal advice. Did you discuss in the meetings that you went to detaining and placing into camps citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This issue was not a legal issue and did not concern any regulations. If there was such a meeting where this was discussed, I did not attend that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss your former boss, or the person you collaborated with, the president of the municipality, Muhamed Cehajic, did you discuss where he was in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I understand. Whether I talked to Cehajic to see where he was in 1992? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attended meetings of the Crisis Staff. This was the power that took over the Municipal Assembly headed by Muhamed Cehajic. You had worked with Muhamed Cehajic and had an office 10 metres from him. Dr. Stakic was now sitting in his office. Did you discuss the fate of Muhamed Cehajic in 1992 in your meetings with the Crisis Staff and Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. These issues, I'm not familiar with the fact whether these issues were, in fact, discussed. But when the takeover took place, that meant that Mr. Cehajic was out of office. The information I had, I knew that he was at home for a while. Later on, I heard that he had been in Omarska. I heard this from his wife who asked me what I knew about it. And I told her that I didn't know much really. And I was not in a position to know. It was outside the scope of my activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a lawyer, did you discuss the legality of the takeover of power with the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nor was I consulted concerning this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a lawyer, did you discuss setting up camps in Prijedor, in particular, the Keraterm and Omarska camps with members of the Crisis Staff, and particularly Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer will be the following: I was never able to find out, even if as just an ordinary citizen, I did try to find out how this all came about. I was never able to obtain any information as to how this had come about and who had taken the decision to set up these camps. The other citizens in Prijedor -- no one really knows this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think there has been testimony from people that know this in this trial. But sir, can you tell us, did you discuss with Simo Drljaca the orders of the Crisis Staff or communicate with him in any way regarding the orders of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps on one occasion when he was charged with assisting the tax collection organs to carry out their task and collect the taxes. It was not possible to do this without members of the police assisting the tax officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question dealt with the camps and detention of citizens. Did you discuss with Simo Drljaca or communicate with him in any way orders of the Crisis Staff regarding the camps? And I'm talking about the facilities. I don't want to play any language games. I'm talking about the facilities in Omarska and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How he received his instructions, I don't know. I never spoke to him about it except once, I intervened with him for an acquaintance of mine, a judge, Omer Kerenovic. I asked Mr. Drljaca to have this person released from the camp. That was the first and last time I went to his office, to ask for this. I never returned to see him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see an order or were you -- did you have knowledge of an order from the Crisis Staff that no one could be released from the camps without the approval of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this. The way -- what was done was probably not accessible to people like me or other simple officials. If there were any such, I don't know whether it was published anywhere, but yes, it's possible that there were. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some very concrete questions about the meetings of the Crisis Staff. If you could confine your answers to the questions, we could move more quickly. Who took the minutes of the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Spiro Marmat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were those minutes kept, and do you have any knowledge of where they are today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the rule was for the minutes to be placed in the files, the files used to keep Municipal Assembly documents, just like in the period before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is your answer you don't know where they are today? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't know, because I left in 1993, where these files were taken later. I really couldn't say what their later fate was. This was mostly done by typists and another employee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who presided over -- let me start again. Is it correct that Dr. Stakic presided over the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the decision that had been made, he was the president of the Crisis Staff, yes. He had a deputy, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present at the meetings of the Crisis Staff that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the decision lists members of the Crisis Staff, those were all municipal officials, including those who were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. I'm going to stop you because that's not my question. My question is: Who was present in the room when you were there that you recall now? Name those people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult now for me to recall. I didn't give it much thought to memorise this or to burden myself with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me give you some names and see if they remind you of people you saw in the Crisis Staff. Did you see Simo Drljaca at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was supposed to attend regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that answer yes, you recall seeing him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, just like I said a minute ago, when he was requested to provide a car and technical support for the tax collectors, yes, he was there. But whether anything else was discussed but it was nothing related to Omarska or -- that probably was not discussed in my presence. If it ever was discussed indeed, I don't know. I can't provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, just answer the question. Was Radmilo Zeljaja present at the meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the Crisis Staff. And from time to time, whenever he could, I guess, yes, he was there. But there were cases when if I attended the meeting, he was there, too, while he was there in that position. While he was still occupying his position, the position he had, he was supposed to be there, yes. And I said there was a representative of the military who was a member of the Crisis Staff, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Colonel Vladimir Arsic at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing him there except a very problematic meeting of the Crisis Staff before, before the Crisis Staff. That's before the Crisis Staff was established, when certain problematic issues were discussed among the deputies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I correct you're talking about before the takeover on the 30th of April or are you discussing after --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely, prior to the takeover. That's when I saw him at one of the meetings. It was more a question of providing information on some issues discussed by the assembly. Security situation, that sort of thing. That's when he gave his assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're talking about 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the Crisis Staff was established, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're talking about the period after the formation on January the 7th of 1992 of the Serbian Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the decision that was taken. The Crisis Staff began to operate at a later point as a Crisis Staff. The assembly, the assembly of the Serbian people, did operate, but the Crisis Staff only began to operate later on when difficulties arose concerning the continuation of the assembly's meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For mandatory reasons, the trial stays adjourned until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. May the usher please bring in the witness immediately. For the record, we can identify Ms. Sutherland supervising Mr. Koumjian this afternoon, once again. And as I heard it, it will be possible to proceed longer today, but prerequisite would be, of course, that the OTP doesn't make use of the entire 90 minutes we have available now. I would say it would be fair just to envisage 45 minutes, and then the remaining time for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll only use 45 minutes. I'm not sure about the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, proceed in the way you started. Mr. Baltic, thank you for coming in. The same rules apply now. If you manage really to concentrate on short answers, we will be able to conclude today. Everything depends on your short answers, short but precise. Thank you. Please, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first become aware that power in Prijedor had been taken from the government headed by Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but I think it was sometime in April. I remember that it was towards the end of April that I -- that when I went to work, I saw at the entrance to the municipal building a colleague of mine who could not enter, who could not come to work. He was a Muslim, a Bosniak by ethnicity, and he asked me what this was all about. And I said, I don't know. Go home, and I'll give you a call. So called him the next day, and he came to work. I had two more Muslims working with me. They all worked until they, themselves, decided to leave. I didn't have anything to do with it, nor was I criticised by anyone for taking that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without adding any more information, can you give me those three names. First the man you spoke to out in front of the building, and then the other two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Smail Kuruzovic, Munevra Nezic, a man by the family name of Dracic. I cannot remember his first name, but he was chief of Mr. Cehajic's cabinet. I think that those were the three individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that short answer. Now, you were allowed into the building that day. Correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I got in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in power that day? What was the authority that was governing Prijedor on that day? And if you allow me, the date that you're talking about we believe in this courtroom is the 1st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're referring to the assembly, the Municipal Assembly, you mean that it was at that time that the Serbian Municipality started to function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is part of my question. Was the Crisis Staff in power on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff appeared later on, after the problems arose. There was an attack on Prijedor, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in power in May -- well, let me ask you another question. When did the assembly that you're talking about, the Serbian Assembly -- isn't it true that it did not meet in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that at the moment. But if it was in April, President Cehajic was no longer -- I mean, if President Cehajic was no longer at the municipality, then instead of that assembly, there must have been already the Serbian Assembly. Whether it was in session -- I believe it was because now I remember the decision reached in the month of May. It was in late May that the decision on the Crisis Staff was reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're speaking about the decision about the formation of the Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at least I think that it was at that period of time. I've already looked at it here, but perhaps we can refresh our memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- who formed, who authorised, the formation of a Crisis Staff or war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor was in power, then Mr. Stakic was the president of the Municipal Assembly. But I don't know how the proposal and the initiative came about, how it was decided that the Crisis Staff should be established because, according to the statute, it was the war presidency that was supposed to function in the situation of imminent danger of war or extraordinary circumstances. Of course, the old title could have been kept, but for formal reasons, I assume the name was changed into Crisis Staff. The composition remained more or less the same as the composition of what was before the Crisis Staff, that is, the presidents and the heads of various departments and so on and so forth. I think that the decision makes mention of who the members are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, please keep your answers short. Sir, going back to the Crisis Staff meetings, where did they take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the small conference room of the assembly, that is, next to the president's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would the Crisis Staff meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer, but I believe it was according to the needs. It is possible that they met twice a week, but I think that in the subsequent period of time, it was not that often. It all depended, of course, on the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that there were times, from what you said, when the assembly could not meet, and even times when the Crisis Staff was not meeting, but decisions had to be made. Isn't that true? Daily decisions would have to be made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was possible for the Crisis Staff to meet because all of the officers in charge at the municipality were there. Apart from them, there was only the representative of the military, that is, the representative of the local barracks. He would show up representing the army. And the others were as I said. Yes, there was also a deputy. He was a member of the Crisis Staff. I mean, others were there. They could meet if necessary on a daily basis, but I don't think that they met every day. Maybe every other day or -- at least at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the assembly could not meet, you indicated there was a time, you say, that the Crisis Staff -- there was a lag between the takeover and the formation of the Crisis Staff, if I understand you. They didn't happen at the same time. During that period of time, when decisions had to be made, who made those decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that period of time, as I told you, at least that was the period of time that you asked me about, after April, after that, in May, we have the decision on the Crisis Staff. So after that, all formal conditions were fulfilled for the Crisis Staff to meet. But it did not start working immediately as a Crisis Staff. I think that it started working as a Crisis Staff after the attack on Prijedor which took place sometime in late May. After this attack, it was already difficult for the assembly to meet, so the Crisis Staff began to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown S180B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm about to show you a decision, you looked at it earlier, S180B. You looked at it earlier today. That's a decision I think you'll recognise in which they are talking about the assembly of the Serb Municipality, according to the Gazette that you edited, met on the 20th of May and passed a decision on the organisation and work of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff. So isn't it correct that that decision -- I'll wait for you to have the document. According to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does he have the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the first decision, Number 18, I believe it appears on the first page, it indicates that that decision on the organisation and work of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff was made on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What am I supposed to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that correct, the Gazette indicates that a decision was passed on the 20th of May? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know I was not able to give you the precise date, but I said I believed that it was around the 20th or the 25th. Now, I can see that it took place on the 25th -- I'm sorry, on the 20th. But as I told you, the decision was reached, was adopted, in the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, we are speaking on the basis of Exhibit 276B. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What I have -- mine is labelled 180. It's the actual Gazette. Perhaps you have the copy of a decision. I showed the witness the Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can agree that we are discussing volume Number 1 of 20 May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some of the people attending the Crisis Staff. Did Slobodan Kuruzovic attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which session you have -- which meeting you have in mind. This document concerns the work of the staff, but there is another decision which specifies who the members were. So his name must be amongst those names as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm not asking you what the decision says. But at the meetings you attended, did you see -- did you see Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he attended every meeting that I attended, but I remember seeing him from time to time. I don't know exactly whether he was present at all of them because I didn't attend all of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the decision that is in front of you, it indicates that the session of the assembly is the 20th of May. Would that have been the first time that the Prijedor, the Serb Municipality of Prijedor Assembly met following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to this decision, according to the introductory parts, underneath Number 18, pursuant to Article --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. Because here we see the phrase "the Municipality of Prijedor." We don't read the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor. But of course it is logical that this decision was adopted by the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is just this, if you can answer it: Was this the first time that the assembly met following the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just see the date, the 20th of May. No, I don't know whether there was another one, whether this was possible. But the takeover, as I said, took place in late April. It is possible that there was one more but I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly building that you were in, what was the name of the street that it was on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mosa Pijada.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the SUP building, the police station, in relation to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the street, opposite the municipality building. These are actually very similar buildings, and there's only this one street between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a map. It's actually a blowup of the map Your Honour -- or actually, I think the map Your Honour used this morning is a reduction of this map. And may this be marked -- perhaps you want to use the same number with a dash?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please -- this is S2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is labelling in English. I should indicate that before I show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I ask that the usher put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at it. If you could look at the buildings marked 10 and 11. And first, I have a yellow marker. If you could take that, and if you can recognise it, mark, highlight, the Municipal Assembly building, if you recognise it. If you could turn, sir, to your left. Do you recognise the buildings -- and they are off screen right now, but marked 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 10, as far as I can tell, is the building of the municipality and the Ljubija iron ore mine. Across the street, we see Number 11. So there must be something there as well. The position of the building is not very clear. I don't know how old this plan is. But the building was right across the street, and the street was Mosa Pijada. Behind that building was the building of the local court. Let me see. Just a second. Yes, yes. I apologise. It's possible that Number 11 is the municipal building, and Number 10 is maybe the building of the MUP and the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to mark it because they have numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said you continued to go to work throughout 1992. Do you recall seeing lines of citizens in front of the police station during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But not in front of the police station, but in front of the building where the national defence secretariat was. People went there to get a permission to leave, and such permissions were issued to them upon their own request. And it was based on this permission that they were able to leave Prijedor in their private cars and take with them whatever belongings they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see those lines of people from the entrance to the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure one could see that because it was right next to the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the summer of 1992, those were almost all women that were in the line. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can say that there were only women there. It was mixed. It is possible that sometimes they were the majority. But during the day, mostly men went there. The people who were looking for this paper. Anyone could request such a permission on behalf of their family, and the permission was not only issued in respect of individuals, but in respect of entire families, depending on who was there, who was applying for the permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see lines of women in front of the police station looking for information about their husbands and sons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the reason why people were there, because the building had two entrances. One could enter the building through both of these doors and get to the premises of the national defence secretariat or somewhere else. I don't know what the reason was why they went there. I just know that it was there that the permission to leave the area -- permissions to leave the area were issued. It is possible that the majority of them were women because if men didn't want to show up for some reason, then their wives went. I couldn't think of any other reason, I mean, I wasn't ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your job that you did in 1992 as the secretary of the municipality of Prijedor and as the editor of the Prijedor Official Gazette, did you falsify any documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't falsify anything. It is possible that such a thing happened with my colleagues. I trusted them. I didn't check what they wrote and published in the Official Gazette. I had confidence in them. So I must say that there was a possibility that such a thing was published in the Official Gazette, but everything that was adopted at the sessions of the Municipal Assembly or, later, the Crisis Staff, had to be published. And the minutes were always checked and verified at the next session. And the deputies would always react in cases of problems if their intervention, for example, had been omitted. And then appropriate corrections would be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone accuse you, as the person for the service, accuse you of falsifying documents or publishing documents that were false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked -- we talked a little bit this morning about the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You're aware that Prijedor was part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know an individual by the name of Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of him, yes. I think he was a deputy even as far back as 1991. I think that's how I heard his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Brdjanin visiting Prijedor in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, but I do not know of any such visit. It could have been announced to certain people only, the people in power. And I was not a person in power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall individuals from the municipality of Prijedor, the top leadership, going to Banja Luka for meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no way for me to know this. I know that earlier, in 1991, and in 1992, people did go because we always requested assistance from the larger towns. And that was the same in the period preceding this. We did not know how they went about a number of things, so we went there to find out about that, too. They had better-qualified personnel, so it was only logical for us to appeal to them for assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall Dr. Stakic going to Banja Luka following the takeover in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never told anything about that. I was not familiar with his whereabouts or where he was going, especially concerning these things that I was not really familiar with. He -- it may have been necessary for him to go, but even in the earlier period. But with what intention exactly, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, prior to testifying, after you received your summons here, did you discuss with anyone the fact that you were coming and questions you might have to address in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not even sure that I would come. Because I requested -- I accepted to come and testify, but I tried to do this via a videolink. I was summoned, and I expected that my request would be granted. But then they handed me a summons. I spoke to your representatives from the section in charge of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct that when you came to court, you greeted Dr. Stakic as someone that you knew? You smiled and nodded at him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I greeted everyone. He's a living creature, too, for me now. Whether he is guilty or not, that's up to the Court to decide. Even if I knew he was, I would still -- I had a photograph taken last night down at the beach with a security guard, just for the sake of my son and daughter getting some fun. I greeted you, too, the first day before the hearing began just like I greeted everyone else. I like all the people in this room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you haven't had any conflicts with any of the people in this room? I hope I've treated you correctly. But other than just answering questions, you have not had any conflicts with Dr. Stakic, in particular, I'm talking about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember. But we didn't meet very often, and he may not have had a favourable opinion of me. But he'd sometimes tell me that I was a rather good man, not a bad man. The first time I saw him was in 1991. I had no idea. He was younger, and I heard where he was from and that he was a physician. And he had his own job. I had my own job. So I really had no interest in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe the relationship between Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kovacevic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those were mostly people who were the top-ranking people. If you look at it that way, the police back then and now, for us, was a force we had to respect. The president of the assembly, the vice-president -- the president of the executive committee, we know that this is the -- that these are the people in power in the municipality. And even if you don't like them, you had to cooperate with them. You had to work together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see them -- in order to do their work, would you see them meeting together and conferring in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if the executive board was reviewing material for the session -- for a session of the assembly, even the president himself could request an issue to be put on the agenda because before that was done, you could not convene a session. So they had to work together. That was true at an earlier stage as well as now. These were -- these are the two people who worked together the most. And if it weren't for that, there would be no executive board and there would be no assembly. That would probably provide a reason for replacements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it the responsibility of the chief of police to keep the president of the municipality informed of his activities, and during 1992, to comply with the orders of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a short answer. Every organ had its own field of competence, and the police had to do its work according to their regulations. But they did have a line -- a chain of responsibility. And this didn't mean that the president of the Crisis Staff could not do their job more efficiently with the chief of police. There were cases where people fired shots in cafes and out in the street. So that had to be stopped by the police. So that was not done efficiently, well, then -- and there were other such cases, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, weren't you tasked, weren't you given the responsibility by the Crisis Staff to contact Mr. Drljaca and to obtain a report from him on the implementation by the police of the conclusions, that is, the orders, decisions, rulings, and conclusions of the Crisis Staff? Isn't it true you wrote him letters in the summer of 1992 asking him to forward that report to you, and you were acting on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll give you the following answer: The work of the assembly -- during the work of the assembly, we always asked questions about how certain decisions were implemented, and they were implemented by organs -- administrative organs. Technical services could not obtain this information, whether certain decisions were implemented or not. If there was a request to get an opinion concerning that, and if it was up to the technical services to do that, in order for us to learn whether there were any such conclusions, we could have requested this information. But my only request could have been to the effect whether a certain organ received certain conclusions or not. If we got ours, we considered our job done. But if we wanted to obtain reliable information on how someone was implementing their conclusions, then we would have had to go to those persons directly to see whether they implemented certain decisions and obtain our information on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that general explanation. But I'm asking you concretely about Mr. Drljaca and the decisions of the Crisis Staff. So, sir, perhaps to refresh your recollection, to be fairer to you, I would like to show you some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe it's 65 ter number 271. And I'd like the ELMO to first have the document put on the ELMO 00633804. Apparently Ms. Karper informs me that this is not part of the 65 ter, but there are two consecutive ERNs, and it appears that it's one document. I'll hand both pages to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For technical reasons, I want to emphasise that the document earlier - you can proceed - mentioned as S2-1. For today, it has to have DP, the next available DP number, and also this new document, the second-next DP number. And in addition, this brings me to the fact that 65 ter Number 271 was not yet discussed. We had it on the ELMO, and we have it on the transcript. But for the purposes of the deposition, it has the number DP/J-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if Your Honour had the complete document or was missing the second page because apparently our original 65 ter was missing the second page. But we have them to hand out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the ELMO, I hope, now is 00633804. It's a letter, and it correct that you are the person who signed this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The letter dated 23rd of June, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delivered directly to Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the booth, we have a technical problem and don't have anything on our video screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll proceed -- should I proceed to question the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there's handwriting on that letter. Do you recognise the handwriting on that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I do. This is clearly visible. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the handwriting next to the decisions, do you recognise that writing? Is that yours also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this letter you sent on behalf of the Crisis Staff to Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know really, but probably. I was requested to request something like this from Mr. Drljaca. And this letter was written, but that's just what I'm trying to explain, what I said earlier, we don't know whether something was implemented or not. So we wanted him to write down all the conclusions by date and number whether those conclusions were implemented or not. But what specifically is written here, I really don't know. And then after that job of his, this was supposed to be reviewed by the Crisis Staff. But no matter whether it was sent there or not, every second or third day when they had meetings, they orally informed about the conclusions that had been adopted being implemented or not, so there was no need to do this in writing. Whether later on at some point someone did, in fact, do it in writing, it's impossible to say but just looking at this letter because this is only a request for Simo Drljaca to speak out on these conclusions. One thing is for sure: This was sent by the technical services, but it's not because I wanted it. Someone requested me to prepare this for one of the next meetings of the Crisis Staff, to have this in writing. Although at every meeting, people would refer to these conclusions and say whether any of those conclusions had indeed been implemented or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question, then, and correct me if I'm wrong: You didn't decide yourself that you were going to make Simo Drljaca give this report? Somebody told you to get this information from Mr. Drljaca. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only way, because I was not interested in this. If someone made a request for me to do this, I can't tell you now who this was specifically. But it would only have been logical for someone in a leading position within the staff, or maybe a deputy. That seems a logical assumption to make. We can't know for sure now whether it was the one or the other, but I believe it was the first man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could just look at the previous page and just confirm that -- I believe His Honour showed that to you earlier -- that is, again, a letter that you sent on behalf of the Crisis Staff for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And that, for the record, is ERN Number 00633803.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must connect these two documents because both are about providing information on the implementation of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, this is DP/J --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's only several days between these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it appear that -- please read it over and tell me, am I correct that the letter, the smaller letter, was sent after you did not receive a response to the longer letter listing the decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my conclusion, too, because this smaller one appears to be urgent because there was no answer to -- received to the first letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me something, if you can, sir: Were all the decisions of the Crisis Staff written down? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, but it doesn't mean that they necessarily were. Those that were recorded in the minutes were then copied, and then those minutes were forwarded - I'm not sure if they were, but I suppose so - and then they got the minutes for the next session and they could have looked to see whether there were any omissions. And aside from that, I can't know what else was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Because you weren't present at all the meetings, and if it wasn't written down and given to you, you wouldn't know? You can just answer if that's correct or not correct --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I think you're right. If I wasn't there, I can't know. Aside from these decisions, whether it was possible for any other decisions to be there that were never recorded in writing, only those persons who decided on these issues can know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you publish all of the written decisions that you received from the Crisis Staff? Were they published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what was done after a meeting by the Crisis Staff, when the record had been compiled, that was -- it was necessary to put together a sufficient number of such decisions for them to be published in the Official Gazette. If any of the decisions were omitted, well, yes, quite possible something like that may have happened. I don't know whether there were any such omissions or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not receive any objections to this effect myself from any of the sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the longer letter that ends in the Numbers 3804, the second decision, 02-111-127/92, which apparently was dated the 4th of June, 1992, and as indicated in the handwriting, this decision concerns the forbidding of the release of prisoners, would you have any explanation, sir, for why this decision may not have ever been published in the Official Gazette of Prijedor? And yet, you were required to ask Mr. Drljaca if he had complied with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, judging by this longer letter, I can see those conclusions enumerating -- enumerated. And there was someone who took notes and recorded what happened. But if it happened indeed like you said, that this was related to the ban on the release of prisoners, but if there was any trace of this in the minutes, we should go to the minutes and look there. If not, there may have been something outside the minutes. That's the most probable thing. I can't think of any other possibility. The minutes from that particular meeting itself should show which decisions were taken. And if this is one of the conclusions included, then it would, indeed, be from that meeting officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, I'm trying to finish in the next five minutes. But let me tell you: If you find those minutes, please, let me know. You indicated you were a lawyer and were asked at times by the Crisis Staff for legal advice. Did they ask you questions about legality of the appropriation of property of the citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never consulted. But I was familiar with certain interventions to stop requisition or plundering, as they said, of property that had been abandoned. I think we saw a document here requesting measures to be stepped up to provide better security and for all of that to be brought and put into one place if that was mobile property, to be kept in one place and guarded in that one place. Because of course, if people had an opportunity, they would seize it and just grab those things, and we refer to those people as profiteers. Of course, some sort of -- what should I call it -- platoon was established quite aside from official security because even within the police, you know that they could take part in this, so this was all to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you raised a question. In fact, you looked this morning at two copies of a decision setting up an intervention platoon. And the only difference between what was signed and what was published was the sentence saying that the members would be selected by the Crises -- approved by the Crisis Staff. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was possible, for example, that someone had a certain vested interest in having his people appointed there. That's a different thing. But if I was in a position to have my people appointed, then I could have an agreement with these people for things to be done my way and in my own interests. So that's also the explanation why certain people wanted it to be not really -- well, on the one hand, for more people to be involved and for people to be appointed who wanted to do an honest job. There may have been problems -- there could have been problems there about who was to set up such bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did the Crisis Staff consult you on the legality of requiring citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality, citizens of Prijedor, to renounce all of their property before being allowed to leave the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear this. The question was never regulated specifically. The constitution guaranteed the freedom of movement and the right to own property. I'm not excluding the possibility that someone may have requested a thing like that, but I don't think that I was the one to whom such a question could be addressed. I mean, I didn't have any interests of the kind. I mean, I didn't try to make any profit out of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- I had only one question, but Ms. Sutherland reminded me, I did have a video queued -- excuse me, I have two more questions. A video queued, which has been previously played. I believe it's S7. And I was going to ask if I could get five more minutes, ask the witness to identify the persons sitting around the table. Could that be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Baltic, would you identify on the screen starting from the right-hand side of the screen the participants that you recognised in that photograph -- in that still of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not really still, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you identify anyone right now from looking at the screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, he did not have it on his screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this image, which was not really still, as far as I can see, there's Karadzic, at least this person looks like Karadzic. If the image should really become still, maybe these other people -- but I don't know. I don't see them. I don't think I could recognise them. I don't know these people from what I can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the video unit to try to have a real still. Maybe move a little bit forward and backward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we can perhaps, then, play the video, and then we will go back to it, sir. We're going to play a minute or so of this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you recognise anyone on that video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes. The people with whom I worked ever since 1991. I saw Kovacevic, the president of the executive board; Dragan Savanovic, the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, later Crisis Staff; the secretary for the national defence, Mr. Slavko Budimir. I also saw, but the image is no longer here, either Zeljaja or Arsic, because for a period of time one of them occupied this function, and then the other one took over. I'm not sure, but this should have been during that period of time. This is so far as I could tell. But again, I no longer have image on the screen. I recognised the people that I told you about, and according to the statute, they were members of the Crisis Staff -- and yes, I forgot, Simo Drljaca, and Stakic was there as well. I don't see others. Pursuant to the decision on the Crisis Staff, there should be other people as well, I mean, the number specified. I see Slavko Budimir facing me on the left side of the image. Then Stakic to my left. And Drljaca or Bosko Mandic, I'm not sure. But he was the vice-president of the executive board. I don't know these other people whose profiles we can see on the image. Those were the municipality officials who were present there pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, we have now before us 11.36.24.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could back up about 5 seconds, please, before we play it again. Could the booth back up the tape about 5 seconds or so. Okay. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to play the tape again, and if you recognise people and want to identify them, please say "stop."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You can stop now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here are the people I told you about a moment ago. Right in front of me, we can see the president of the assembly, that is, the Crisis Staff, Mr. Stakic. Next to him is Slavko Budimir. As far as I can see, the others are not really visible. I cannot recognise them. Maybe you have another picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll continue to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see the first person from the right, again, the image is flickering, but I think that this is -- can the -- can this flickering be stopped, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karadzic, although he looks a bit younger. I don't know the person sitting next to him, the one wearing glasses. And the one after, no, I don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no, no. I apologise. I said Karadzic, but actually the person looks like Zeljaja, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see Simo Drljaca, Kovacevic, Vojo Pavicic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the person on the right now wearing civilian clothes? Just on the very right of the screen next to Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wearing civilian clothes, I think this is Pavicic, Vojo Pavicic, who was in charge of town planning, the secretary of that department. Sitting to the right of Kovacevic is the person whom I cannot see clearly, these two individuals. I don't think I'm able to identify them. You have the same image from a different angle maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can watch when we play it. Is the first one in uniform Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You can play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he reminds me of him a little. But the beard is somewhat long -- the chin is a bit longer. And he has got more hair. Here I can see Arsic next to the person talking. This is Dragan Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Savanovic the one with the beard that was writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The image is no longer there. I think he has a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could reverse, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just saw a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Dragan Savanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the civilian clothes on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't paying attention to the clothes -- yes, yes, in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on very quickly. Did you know someone by the name of Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kondic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kondic. No. Maybe by sight, but I don't know who he was or what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document I'd like to have marked as an exhibit. It's not on the 65 ter list, but since it came up in the last -- the name came up in the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think a final document from the OTP. May we have the -- during the time the documents are distributed, the DP numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The map initially numbered S2-1 is DP-9. The next document with the ERN ending 804 is DP-10. And this document will be DP-11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a Vinko Kondic who in 1992 was the head of the police following the takeover in Kljuc Municipality and later became a member -- let me just leave it at that. And also a member of the Kljuc Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. This is the first time I hear about such person. But maybe if I were to see him, I would recognise him. Maybe I know the man by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during all of the time that you worked in Prijedor in 1992, attended meetings of the Municipal Assembly, if you can -- I'm not going to ask you any questions about that document, so you don't need to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we have a copy of the document as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was just handed to you yesterday, but you can have my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the last question. In 1992, you told us that you went to your office every day in the Municipal Assembly building, that on occasions you attended meetings of the Crisis Staff, You attended meetings of the Municipal Assembly, that your office was on the same floor as that of the president of the municipality and the president of the executive board. During all of the meetings that you had with these individuals, did you ever discuss the killings of hundreds of citizens of non-Serbian ethnicity in Prijedor and the destruction, the burning and arson, of thousands of homes of non-Serbian citizens in Prijedor? Did you discuss those crimes in your meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there, no. But as a private citizen outside the work, I was in a position to hear of such things as having happened in Keraterm. They concerned certain individuals. But that such an issue was discussed, no, at least not in my presence. Not in front of me. I'm not excluding the possibility that in certain circles, there were such discussions. But I never had the opportunity of being present at any such conversation in the municipality or outside the municipal building. Prijedor is a small town, and news travels fast. And I must say, I must admit, that I did hear things. But it was not published in the media. But I did hear such stories. I heard of one such case, for instance, in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the agenda of these meetings which you indicated to us was set by the president of the municipality discussed such problems as the distribution of fuel, but never discussed problems such as the killings of hundreds or thousands of your fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was never any discussion about this last issue, whether he on his own decided on the agenda of the Crisis Staff, I don't know. All I know was that we never received draft agendas in advance. It was never requested that the technical services, for instance, prepare the relevant material or that the members of the Crisis Staff would receive such an agenda in advance. Only very few people worked there, only those who were necessary, because I can see from the minutes, for instance, that there was a meeting on this particular date, then on the following day. But then meetings were not held as often in the later period of time. I suppose that the president consulted with someone as to what should be on the agenda. I don't know who it could have been. But at any rate, later on, the agenda would be recorded. This would be part of the minutes, and this is how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot say I don't have more questions. But I can say that given the time limitations, I've completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I, therefore, give immediately the floor to the Defence. And please, take into account that the first portion should not be longer than about 20 minutes, and then after a break, you will have 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Baltic. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic and Mr Danilo Cirkovic, I'm defending Mr. Stakic before this Tribunal. I also have time restrictions; that is, I only have a given period of time, amount of time, during which I can questions of you. I know that you are -- you must be tired, and I will try to finish with these questions as quickly as possible. I should first like to try and clear up certain issues that were brought up during these proceedings. Just one remark: We speak the same language, so I should kindly ask you to pause after I have finished my question before you proceed with your answer so that the interpreters have enough time to interpret. It is possible that you will find some of the questions common knowledge, but we have to show to this Tribunal, we have to demonstrate, how the system that we are talking about functioned because the way it worked is not familiar to all of the participants in these proceedings. Mr. Baltic, who did you answer to for your work as the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president is the most senior official. Then comes the vice-president. They chair the sessions. They lead the assembly, and they represent the assembly. I was also one of the officials appointed by the same assembly as they were, and as such, I was responsible, first of all, to the assembly itself. And of course, should -- if I failed to appear, to attend, a session of the Municipal Assembly, I don't think that the president could actually relieve me of my duty on its own. But I'm sure -- I mean, he could not appoint me or relieve me of my duty. He could only make comments or criticism of my work. But I was responsible to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The record doesn't reflect what you said a moment ago. Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The body that elected me, that is, the Municipal Assembly. It was the Municipal Assembly that appointed me to my position, and it was the Municipal Assembly that could relieve me of my duty for appropriate reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like the usher to give the witness Exhibit Number D3, please. It's a statute of the Prijedor Municipality, draft version, because we don't have the final version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baltic, will you please turn to Article 51 so that we can read in the statute what you just said a moment ago. Would you be so kind and read out Article 51.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Article 51 reads as follows: "The assembly secretary shall be accountable to the assembly for his work and for the work of the assembly services," as I just indicated a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now please turn to Article 40. Can you please read Article 40 for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The president of the Municipal Assembly shall represent the assembly." Item Number 2: "The president of the assembly shall convene and organise assembly sessions and preside over them or chair them. The president of the assembly may initiate debates on matters within the competence of the assembly. The president of the assembly shall submit proposals for general enactments and reports, information, analysis, and other documents addressed to the assembly, to the working bodies of the assembly." There's more: "The president shall hear the solemn declarations by the officials elected or appointed by the assembly unless otherwise prescribed by the statute. The president of the assembly shall perform other tasks as defined by the statute."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the working material here in front of us because we were never able to obtain the final version. Does this correspond to the statute in accordance with which you worked at the time you were the secretary of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it does because the previous statute was used before July 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the Municipal Assembly, in this case, the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, could he have and perform functions which are not prescribed by this statute, or is it the case that he could only perform those functions provided for in respect of him by the statute of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the municipality -- the president of the assembly had to work in accordance with the law, and the statute provided for his duties and obligations. If he worked in a different manner, if he acted differently, and if this became known to the deputies of the assembly, they could ask for his removal if the violations in question were of a more serious nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously the statute of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly - at least I wasn't able to find such a provision - did not provide for the president of the Municipal Assembly to command the police. In the course of your work, did you at any point in time see Mr. Cehajic issue any order to the head of the police, to Mr. Talundzic, which he was obliged to carry out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember any such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Stakic issue such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not an example like this. But here yesterday was the first time I ever got to see that order requesting from the Ministry of the Interior to perform their security duties to citizens and property in a more efficient manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the municipality, could he -- could he send an appeal without going into the exact form, wording, of this enactment we have in front of us here? For example, if there were races in town, for example, in peacetime, could he ask for -- could he ask the chief of the police to provide security for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it was implicit for the president to do this because everyone worked within their own framework and regulations. The MUP, the police, worked according to their own regulations within their own framework. If there was a festivity or some sort of a party in the municipality, of course the police were there to provide security, to close certain streets down to traffic and to make sure that everything went smoothly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that the police had its own chain of command and responsibility which did not depend on the municipal organ's seat and the chain of command of the police? Did it actually not go through the channels, the command channels, of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the earlier period, because there were no laws, laws cannot be changed, amended, and passed in a quick fashion, especially as regards the police and the military. The command, it comes from the top down. The local representatives of the government, according to law and according to their moral obligation, if anything was malfunctioning and if there is general agreement that something was done in an improper way, they were then supposed to ask people to follow laws and prescriptions. And if a certain person refused to do this, he could not take an order except if it was his own will to accept something and work accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should that person not accept to do something requested from him by someone who was not his superior, that person would not be penalised, would he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No such request could be made, but he could ask the assembly to debate the work of that official. And if sufficient grounds were there to initiate the removal, that is, dismissal, of this person but only by the municipal body whose responsibility it was to nominate this official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you believe it's appropriate to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for helping me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's have a break in this deposition taking until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Even though it's not the appropriate time during such deposition taking, is it correct that the OTP wants to withdraw a motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, the Rule 94 -- I think it's 94 bis motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections. Also, not that we do it not in this framework, we all agree that it's withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We all -- actually our side agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At the same time that we're withdrawing this motion, we'll provide copies today and file tomorrow our motion regarding the journalist Gras who we obtained a short statement from on Monday and had previously obtained a short video including an interview with the accused. We believe her testimony would take about one and a half hours on direct examination. That's a real estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do, Your Honour. We haven't read the motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to back this --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, we don't want to steal your time. Please proceed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baltic, the Prosecution asked you the following question: How come you were not mobilised? At that time, meaning 1992 and 1993, did you have a work obligation, and can you please tell us what that entailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During my work in the period you refer to, just like other high officials and directors of companies, and the other personnel in the assembly, we did have a work obligation which meant that we were not allowed to leave our work. Even if we, perhaps, wished to go somewhere and wear uniform. Only if someone decided of their own accord to leave their position and to no longer hold that particular office, then they could apply to go wherever they wanted to go.
