utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us, please, be accurate about this. They could not go wherever they wanted to go; they could either go to the front or hold their position, the position they had, on the basis of their work obligation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The work obligation, what that meant is for you to stay in your job. If you left your position, you would no longer have a job, and it was your legal obligation to go wherever the relevant organs saw fit to send you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The relevant organs, at that time in that area, were the military bodies. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your testimony, the Honourable Chamber did not show you any of the documents, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that you are now testifying without any preparation and only on the basis of what you remember was happening ten years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will show you a document now, and we'll try to clarify a point here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like the usher to show the witness Exhibit S112, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you will be shown this document. I know that it's a bit difficult for you to read this. What we want to know is about this Number 19, the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision on the appointment of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality. On page 58 of today's transcript, line 20, you stated that there was an accurate list contained in this decision as to who the members of the Crisis Staff were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's indeed what I believed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under Number 1, we see the name Milomir Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, appointed president. Number 2, Dragan Savanovic, vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor as vice-president. Number 3, Dr. Milan Kovacevic, president of the executive board of Prijedor Municipality as a member. Slobodan Kuruzovic, commander of the municipal TO staff for Prijedor appointed as member. Bosko Mandic, commander of the municipal staff of civilian protection for Prijedor appointed as a member. Simo Drljaca, chief of the public security station in Prijedor appointed as member. Slavko Budimir, secretary of the municipal secretariat for national defence, Prijedor, member. Ranko Travar, secretary for the secretariat for the economy and social activities of Prijedor, member. Vojo Pavicic, secretary of the municipal secretariat for urban planning, housing, and communal services as well as ownership matters, member. And under Number 10, Dr. Zeljko Matsura [phoen], officer in charge of health and social protection and social activities, Prijedor, as member. What you told us, you said it did happen a number of times that other people attended the meetings of the Crisis Staff, as you yourself did at times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that some other people who were not members of the Crisis Staff could, at times, attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that perhaps give rise to an amount of confusion, you saying that you saw Mr. Zeljaja, and it's quite obvious that his name is not listed as him being one of the members of the Prijedor Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that there is an accurate list according to the respective duties and individually who the members of the Crisis Staff were, is it possible that you made a mistake when you included Mr. Radmilo Zeljaja as one of these members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. Because when I spoke about the decision on the establishment of the Crisis Staff, I did not read through it, so I thought that by that very -- in that decision, names of the members of the Crisis Staff were listed analogous to the members of the war presidency because there you had the list of names of the members of war presidency according that their functions, president and vice-president of the assembly and other officials of the assembly. And then in addition to that, there were some other deputies there. So I may have said something about that, and -- however now, you can see clearly who the members were. They were displayed on the screen here when the video was shown. I named some of those people and here you have them again, their names. But maybe, perhaps, I said that someone was representing the military. I was referring to the commander of the barracks, but I see that his name is not included. It was possible for everyone else to attend, not only members. If for some reason those other people, the nonmembers, were invited to these meetings. So that's exactly what I -- well, now, as I read through this decision on the appointment of the Crisis Staff, I can see clearly that the decision is made pursuant to the decision on the establishment of the Crisis Staff where the respective functions and duties are listed. I had opportunity to look at this decision and here I can see this one now, too, the decision on the nomination of the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said on page, was it 15 or 59 -- page 59, line 15, that there was a deputy who was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I was referring to Srdo Srdic. He was a deputy representative. So that may be my mistake. I thought he was a member of the Crisis Staff, and you can see here that he wasn't. But as a deputy of the assembly, automatically, he was also a deputy of the Municipal Assembly. That's -- I have remembered this just now. Please excuse me for causing this bit of confusion. It was all a long time ago, so I'm trying to recall everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We both accept and understand the reasons for this confusion. So there is no need for you to worry about this. It's quite obvious that you did not prepare for this testimony. Also, on page 61, line 25, the Prosecution asked you the following question -- actually, whether it was true that the Municipal Assembly did not meet in May, and you provided an explanation. We saw the document. It met on the 20th of May. Do you remember that there was a solemn meeting of the Municipal Assembly on the 16th of May, on the occasion of the liberation of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that particular meeting but I know that it was a tradition every year, ever since my childhood, that was the day of the commune, and we always had a ceremonial meeting on that day. But I can't remember whether such a meeting took place in that particular year, too. I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 63, line 12, please do not be confused by this. This is only for the sake of the transcript that I'm giving the page number and the line. We said that the SUP building was across the way from the Municipal Assembly building. Do they directly face one another, or is the municipal building turned sideways somehow to the Ministry of the Interior building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I tried to explain the map that was displayed on the screen, that's exactly what I said. The municipality building faces south by its main entrance, which means that it is turned sideways, in a manner of speaking, to the MUP building, and then directly to the west facing the street there, the Mosa Pijada Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the offices in the Municipal Assembly building, as you sit at your table and work, without actually looking through the window, are you able to see the Ministry of the Interior building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You're not able to do that unless you come out on to the terrace on the south side of the building, looking sideways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You contend that during the period in which the Crisis Staff operated, you did not attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff, is that correct, or at least not the majority of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did attend a number of the meetings, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the members of the Crisis Staff lawyers by profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Vojo Pavicic was a lawyer. He was the secretary for urban planning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to his becoming secretary for urban planning, which tasks was he in charge of? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was the head of a service in charge of legal -- legal property relations. We call it legal property relations or affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No other members of the Crisis Staff were lawyers by profession, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was also the chief, Simo Drljaca, he was a lawyer by profession, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of these events, Dr. Stakic was about 29. Did you know him prior to 1991? I think you already said you didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time that I saw him or heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is not from Prijedor town by origin, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any citizen of Prijedor didn't know him [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not sure. At least I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was Dr. Kovacevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he's older than me. So if I was born in 1941, I think he was two or three years my senior, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time he was probably over 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If we are in 2002 now, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca is younger. He could have been born in 1947 or 1948. He's much younger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we set aside the legal aspect of the matter, I'm careful about phrasing my -- I'm just being careful about phrasing my question. If we set aside the legal aspect of this document, according to the document, the president of the Crisis Staff was Dr. Milomir Stakic. Milomir Stakic, according to you, was he the person to whom all of the questions were addressed, or only some of them, or was it the case that nobody asked him anything? Can you tell us who was the de facto person in charge of this Crisis Staff and what was the position of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: De facto, I don't know who was the person in charge. But in view of the competencies, the work of the Crisis Staff and the work of the Municipal Assembly was presided over by the president of the Crisis Staff and the Municipal Assembly. And the president of the executive board was at the head of the executive board, which consisted of all of the secretaries of various municipal organs, those who had been appointed by the municipality -- by the assembly to various departments. And they formed the executive organ. As I indicated before, during the early period of time, it was the executive board that debated the proposals that came from various departments. If the executive board gave a green light to such a document, then it would be forwarded to the assembly for further discussion. I don't think I can answer your question as to who was the person -- the person in charge because relations were strictly regulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to insist because as His Honour Judge Schomburg indicated, you have the right to say that you don't know the answer to the question. And this would conclude my cross-examination, Mr. Baltic. Thank you very much for coming to testify here. I think that -- I hope that it was our side that gave you the least trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't hope that you have had any trouble at all. But I have to ask if there are any questions in return by the Office of the Prosecutor, based on these line of questions by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Further questioned by The Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this extremely difficult case, and we are faced with a charge of genocide, one could think that the fate of an individual wouldn't count. But I can't conclude this hearing without coming back to a question asked by the Prosecution. This morning, you mentioned that an acquaintance of yours, a judge, Omer Kerenovic, if the transcript is correct, and you stated: "I asked Mr. Drljaca to have this person released from the camp." Can you tell us: What was the fate of Omer Kerenovic? Was he released from the camp and which camp was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. However, during that period of time, I didn't know what his fate was. Later on, I learned about what had happened to him and to a number of other acquaintances of mine, people I met in the street. I tried to find out what their fate was, and it all took a while. I tried to find out from the people I thought would know, from members of the family, from relatives. And the first thing I heard about him was that he had left for Turkey. Later, much later, I'm not quite sure, but I think that somehow I learned that he had been in Omarska, but there was no information -- at least, I wasn't aware of that. But his brother was released shortly after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does this mean that also the brother of Omer Kerenovic was detained in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And once again, the concrete question was: Did you ever see later Mr. Omer Kerenovic? You just told us that you learned that he would be in Turkey. Was it at any point in time confirmed that indeed he survived Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can say is that I did not see him after that. But I don't know from what date, from what day. I don't know when it was that I stopped seeing him. But after all these events were over, I no longer saw him. I don't remember whether someone told me that he had had a rough time or that he had gone to Turkey. I used to know his family. We used to see each other on weekends, and we were on very good terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I understand from this, you have never seen him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the ethnicity of Mr. Omer Kerenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I assume that he was a Muslim, if Turks are Muslims, citizens of Turkey, I mean. But that is from before. I don't know who had come from where, but I think that he is from Turkey by origin. I don't know whether it was his parents who had come from Turkey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I take it from this that you had acquaintances from all ethnic groups, and whether or not you were a good friend with a person at that point in time, that was not relevant whether this person was a Muslim, a Serb, or Croatian person. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct, not only me but others as well. Many of them went to school with me. I have a brother-in-law who is a Muslim. I know people who are acquaintances of mine who are dentists or lawyers, and we never asked who was what. There are approximately 16 different ethnicities in Prijedor, and the participation in the government reflected the composition of the population, which was perfectly normal. These people had various functions, and they socialised together. After this other war, the Second World War, this was forgotten, and the relations were again very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, in addition, why did you address Mr. Drljaca to have this person released from the camp? Why just Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, because Mr. Kerenovic asked me personally to address Mr. Drljaca. Why he had picked him, I don't know. I met him in the street when this happened, and I told him immediately that that was the first time that someone was asking me for help. I realised what it was all about, and I went to see Simo Drljaca because Kerenovic specifically asked me to go and see Drljaca and to ask if he can arrange for his brother to be interrogated as soon as possible, the assumption being that his innocence would be established, that is, that they would conclude that he had not taken part in the conflict and that he would subsequently be released, which is what happened, I think. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, did you address any other person on this issue, on the release of Mr. Kerenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's important not to forget individuals when we are discussing these charges of crimes against humanity, genocide. We are discussing individuals, the fate of numerous individuals, and we have to find out who is responsible -- who is individually responsible for this. And I think you have assisted us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I follow up on your Your Honour's last questions a bit. Specifically, I'd like the witness to look at the book of missing persons, page 231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't ask the witness any further questions. But if there's no objections by the Defence, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May we have S232 shown to the witness, page 231. If that could be put on the ELMO, please. Further questioned by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could focus on number 2024. That's 2021. 2024, please. It's below it. 2024. If you move the book up, I think -- you have to zoom out. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Here we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was Judge Kerenovic, was his name Omer, son of Hamdija, was he born in about 1934, and did he live on Marsal Tita Number 33 in Prijedor? Is that your friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Omer Kerenovic, the judge, was he born in about 1934? Was he about seven years older than you and did he live on Marsal Tita Street in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I have the interpretation, please. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does he have the right channel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not working. Yes, yes I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was your friend Omer Kerenovic, was he the son of Hamdija, was he born about seven years before you in 1934, and did he live on Marsal Tita Street in Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is not my friend, but I knew him as a friend of my father-in-law. I knew he was a judge. And I know that he used to live at this address, Marsal Tita. I didn't know the name of his father. I can see that it's Hamdija, so it must be the name of his father. So I believe that this is him. I've never seen this book. This is the first time that I'm looking at it. But I think that this is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that Mr. Kerenovic was not of Turkish ethnicity, but was a Slav, as you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. But the reason I said that is because I knew that they went there to visit, and that they have family in Turkey. And that is why I said that it is possible that -- but okay, I'm prepared to correct myself. I cannot claim that that's the fact with certainty. I know that he lived in Prijedor and that he was a Muslim. As far as I'm concerned, this was never very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you speak to Simo Drljaca about Judge Kerenovic before or after June the 8th of 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. That was the first time -- I mean the first time I talked to him was during those first days. The people who were initially placed in Omarska, so it must have been during those first days, maybe on the second day. We met in the street accidentally. He works at the court, and we just saw each other in the street. And he asked me that, and I went to see Mr. Drljaca about that. But I never went to the MUP building after that. I never went back, nor did I check whether he had done anything about it, the reason being, I can tell it now, was because it was the first time that I went to see him. I'm sure that there must have been a number of such interventions at the time, and he said it was very difficult for him to work, to act on each such intervention, but I saw that he had made a note of that. So it was my assumption that he would do it. Later, I met --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're not sure about the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Omer, and he didn't tell me anything, whether he was released or not. But I think that he is still alive -- I mean, Omer's brother. I think that he's still alive. I'm not sure but I think he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to learn that Omer Kerenovic, the judge from Prijedor, disappeared from the Omarska camp on June the 8th, 1992, and has never been seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible. It's possible that that happened as well. But I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't see any other questions from the Defence. So therefore, it's for me to express my extreme gratitude that first, on short notice, second without any preparation, you were prepared to come to The Hague and to testify here. There is always a saying that this Tribunal would work in a selective way and work on the basis of witnesses of one ethnicity and the other ethnicity, one for the Defence, one for the Prosecutor. I think your appearance here is an extremely good example that this is not true. And bringing people together from all groups is the only way really to come closer to the truth. I mentioned it earlier. You were not present. We all know that we will never find out the real truth, but we have to come closer. And you assisted us in coming here and giving your testimony, and we all are aware how difficult it is for you to testify in a case when your former president of the Municipal Assembly where you worked as a secretary is an accused person. But nevertheless, we all got the impression that you provided us with so many important additional evidence, facts, and informations that you helped us a lot. And I hope -- you mentioned earlier this afternoon that yesterday, in the evening at the beach, you took a photograph of a guard together with you as a souvenir. And I hope that will be not the only souvenir you are bringing back to Prijedor, but also you can bring the message to the people, all groups in Prijedor, what's going on here and in which way the trials are conducted, and also to encourage other persons to appear here as witnesses. Thank you very, very much for coming and for testifying. This concludes this taking of deposition. And may I ask the usher, please, to escort Mr. Baltic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, say just one sentence. I'm very pleased I helped you, with the fact that I helped you. But I must say that it was quite difficult. I don't like conflicts, be it with ordinary police officers. I was never held responsible for anything, not even a minor traffic violation. I'm very sorry when things of this kind happen. As for Stakic, he was the president of the assembly as far as I'm concerned; he was not my president. I went about doing my job, and he did his. He is here before you. You will see. Let me just thank you once again for giving me the opportunity of saying something. And I think that I will go home in peace. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have a good trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: at 5.20 p.m., followed immediately by a Status Conference 24 25
